Question: Is it true that all animals evolved from a single source? If so, why did they evolve into such a diverse range of species instead of just one?
Answer: Yes, it is true. All organisms on Earth have a single common ancestor, (referred to as ‘LUCA’ - the Last Universal Common Ancestor). They evolved into a diverse range of species as a result of natural selection. When populations of organisms are separated, they stop swapping genes of course. Different mutations occur in different populations, and don’t pass between the different populations, because they are separated. This is called divergent evolution. The separation can be the result of geography or behavior. The population becomes best adapted for the environment where it lives. And it may evolve new looks and shapes that don’t necessarily aid survival, but don’t interfere with it, either. Those may become predominant by chance, or through mate selection. The entire world isn’t just a single environment - it has cooler and warmer areas, water and land, desert and heavy rainfall areas - so life forms in those different places wind up very different from each other.

We find lizards that have evolved tiny limbs or have lost their limbs in such environments today. So, in that type of environment, loss of limbs is selected for. Question: If evolution is true, why hasn't my pet goldfish turned into a shark yet?
Answer: Because evolution works like this: A single species radiates into several new species with different features that are adapted for the different environments the original inhabited. These changes accumulate over time, the radiating species become more and more different from the original, and, often, from each other. But one thing they never, ever do is go BACKWARD. Species evolve to become more different from one another - never LESS different.* Sharks diverged from bony fish around 420 million years ago! No bony fish can ever become anything like a shark. Sharks have skeletons made of cartilage. Only their jaws and teeth are hardened. They have rough skin, and no scales. Goldfish are freshwater fishes with bone skeletons and scales covering their bodies. These are incredibly different animals. Additionally, goldfish are domesticated animals. Their ancestor was a species of carp, but what they are today is the result of selective breeding by humans, not natural evolution. But no matter how long humans selectively breed goldfish, it’s super unlikely they could turn them into anything like a shark. And impossible for them to ever become sharks, because evolution never goes backwards. *By difference, I mean genetic difference, not morphology - species do sometimes evolve to look superficially similar due to adapting to similar niches, but under the skin, where it counts, they’re extremely different.

Question: Why is everyone convinced that the human being is omnivorous when it is clearly frugivorous (does not mean vegetarians), like monkeys? Just look at your teeth and think that eating meat every day will damage your health.
Answer: For starters, being frugivorous and omnivorous are not mutually exclusive things. Frugivory is a subcategory which can be located beneath designations such as ‘herbivore,’ ‘hypocarnivore,’ and ‘omnivore.’ All that ‘frugivorous’ means is that more than 50% of the diet is comprised of fruit. For instance, chimpanzees are frugivores. 60% of their diet is fruit, primarily figs. But 10% of their diet is animal foods, including insects and monkeys. Chimpanzees are hypocarnivores as well as frugivores. Humans, on the other hand, are not frugivores, because with few localized exceptions, humans don’t have a diet that is more than 50% fruit, and they never have. Instead, humans have evolved to eat a diet primarily of cooked tubers, shoots, roots, greens, and seeds, with some nuts and fruits, and around 30% of their calories on average coming from animal foods (mainly meat in hunter-gatherer cultures). Humans have had fire since Homo erectus, so their digestive systems have evolved to cope efficiently with cooked, not raw, food. And they are predatory omnivores, highly adapted to large game predation, with a shoulder joint evolved to allow hard, accurate throwing, and a very efficient cooling system with ample sweat glands that allows them to persistence-hunt during the hottest part of the day. Some human cultures do eat quite a lot of fruit, to be fair… but some eat remarkably little. But I’m unware of any human culture that has ever had a diet of more than 50% fruit. (The San, for example, eat a lot of fruit, but half of the plant portion of their diet is nuts, not fruit). So, not only could a frugivore be an omnivore anyhow, but there is zero evidence that humans are frugivores, or, in fact, that any hominin was a frugivore. In other news, gorillas are also not frugivores. (Nor are they herbivores - they are hypocarnivores, which is a category of omnivore). Human teeth are typical primate teeth, but fairly reduced, because you don’t need strong teeth to eat cooked food that you cut up with a knife. lol.

Name: Donna Fernstrom
Question: Why aren’t there green mammals?
Answer: Mammalian hair has only two types of pigment, and neither can produce the color green. We metabolize chlorophyll, so we can’t concentrate in our skin. The color blue in the vast majority of animals, called Tyndall blue, is produced by light refraction - the structure of the blue surface, rather than by pigment. Add yellow pigment and Tyndall blue, and you get green. (True blue pigment is vanishingly rare, and only a handful of species can produce blue pigment). Mammalian hair doesn’t have the right structure to produce Tyndall blue. But some mammalian skin has evolved to produce it - The skin on the Mandrill’s face is structured to reflect blue light. In dim lighting, it’s just pale/white. Theoretically, if you added yellow pigment to this, you could get green, but why? The blue evolved to attract attention. Green is a camouflaging color in most cases. So, while possible, it’s extremely unlikely to happen. We’ll never know if it has happened in the past, in extinct species, however.

Question: Why don't giraffes stand upright? Wouldn't that increase their height quicker than evolving longer legs/neck?

If a random mutation aids survival and reproduction, then the individual who has it is more likely to survive and reproduce than those who don’t. At some point, longer legs were more advantageous than being able to rear up and reach stuff that way. A giraffe’s current body design makes standing on its hind legs irrelevant, so it can feed with less energy expended.

Name: Donna Fernstrom
Question: Did the dinosaurs go extinct because they had small forebrains?
Answer: No. The dinosaurs did not go extinct. At least, not all of them. We now understand that birds are just one branch of dinosaur. They’re no different from other dinosaurs than bats are different from other mammals. As for what killed the non-avian dinosaurs, that’s easy to answer as well. At the time of the strike, the Deccan Traps, a volcanic area, had been erupting for a while, and this had caused a mass extinction event, though not a huge one. But the changes the volcanism caused were already beginning to slow dramatically by the time the real disaster struck. The non-avian dinosaurs would have survived the Deccan Traps volcanic disaster easily, just as they had survived a series of other mass extinctions since they first evolved. But they couldn’t survive this. The Chicxulub impactor - a massive asteroid slamming into the Earth at the tip of what is now the Yucatan Peninsula. 80% of all species - plants, animals, on land and in the sea - perished. The impact set broad swathes of the Americas on fire, then doused the flames with tsunamis. The skys were filled with sand, ash, and sulfuric acid, blocking the clouds. Tektites, tiny round balls of solidified magma, rained from the sky and choked the gills of aquatic animals. In what is now North America, a dinosaur, torn apart in the mayhem, fell into a low-lying water-filled area along with partially burned vegetation, and dying fish, their gills clogged with tektites. And they were buried, together, that way. Good luck for us. A snapshot in time, fossilized - within days of the disaster itself, if not the very day! Across the world, fault lines slipped, and earthquakes rumbled, causing more tsunamis and more destruction. Setting off more eruptions in the Deccan Traps, and in other places that would otherwise not have all gone off at once. More ash, more sulfuric acid billowing into the air! And then it began to rain - acid raining from the sky. No light. The plants died. The animals followed. Most mammals died. Most dinosaurs died. Most of everything died. The larger they were, the quicker they fell. Large animals need more food. Slowly, the ash fell, the acid was washed from the sky. It left behind a line in the sedimentary rock that we can easily see - a line laced with iridium, an element found commonly in asteroids, but very rare on Earth. As the world began to recover, the remaining 20% of species, greatly reduced in total numbers, began to recover as well, and then to diversify to fill all of the empty niches left behind. Some diversified faster than others, but it took a long time from our perspective. Today, there are more dinosaur species alive than there are mammals species. Reptile brains aren’t structured the same way mammalian brains are. They also have fewer redundancies, and are packed with many neurons. This allows reptiles to be as smart or smarter than mammals even when their brain is quite a bit smaller in overall size than a mammal’s brain. Prior to the K-Pg disaster, dinosaurs had smaller brains. So did mammals. But as we are now beginning to understand, that doesn’t mean they were stupid. Modern reptiles aren’t even remotely as stupid as we used to believe they are. Lizards can learn a maze as well as a mouse. And birds? With their much larger brains? Well, they’re brilliant. Us primates lucked out. Like reptiles, our brains are more densely packed with neurons than those of other mammals. But the most intelligent birds have as many neurons in their forebrain as great apes do, despite the smaller brain size. Only we exceed them. As for the non-avians - we can’t really know how their brains were structured. We only have their skull, and that can tell us a bit about the size and shape of the brain, but not so much how much there was of each part. Not that any of that matters. When a giant rock from space comes calling, all the smarts in the world won’t save you.

Question: Why are birds closer to being a dinosaur than turtles, alligators, lizards, and snakes?

It seems most likely that the first proto-feathers evolved in the Avemetatarsalians that both dinosaurs and pterosaurs evolved from, because they have now found down feathers on a pterosaur. It’s extremely unlikely that the same structures evolved twice, so their joint ancestor must have had them. And it must have been warm-blooded, because ectotherms (cold-blooded animals) don’t have insulation - it would be detrimental to them. Only endotherms and mesotherms have insulation. Some dinosaurs lost their feathers. Very large animals living in a tropical climate have more problems shedding heat than retaining it, so they didn’t need insulation. You see the same thing with rhinos and elephants in Africa. But many dinosaurs had quills, and various types of feathers. There’s not much unique about birds, with that in mind. They’re no different from other dinosaurs than bats are different from other mammals.

Third, the first birds would have evolved from a group of small Maniraptoran dinosaurs that would have been very similar to the first birds - a bunch of different species, but only one leading to the actual first bird. How could we know which one it was, even if by some miracle we had fossils of them all (which we don’t)? All of the small Maniraptoran dinosaurs from the era of the first birds were pretty similar. Question: Are the terms "ape" and "chimp" scientifically accurate?
Answer: The term ‘ape’ is not a scientific term, but generally refers to animals that are in clade Hominoidea. In common language, the term usually refers to all Hominoids other than humans, but may also be used to include all Hominoids including humans. Several languages do not have an analogous term (they do not have separate words for apes and monkeys). So, no, the term ‘ape’ is not scientifically accurate, because its definition is not consistent within the English language, much less within any other languages. The term ‘chimp,’ however, is just a shorthand for ‘Chimpanzee.’ Chimpanzees are Pan troglodytes, and no other animal. The name is a derived form of their name in an unspecified Bantu language dating back to before 1738, when it was first recorded. It is the official common name for this animal in English, and thus is as ‘scientifically accurate’ as any official common name. A great many other languages also use this name, or one that is extremely similar to it, to refer to this animal. However, in scientific papers, this animal will be referred to as Pan troglodytes, as the official taxonomic names for species transcend all languages by design, thus are the same regardless of the language spoken. So, while ‘chimpanzee’ is scientifically accurate enough in English, ‘Pan troglodytes’ is much more accurate. There is an animal that is sometimes colloquially referred to as a ‘pygmy chimpanzee,’ but the official common name for this animal is ‘Bonobo,’ and it is Pan paniscus.

Name: Donna Fernstrom
Question: Why were dinosaurs considered reptiles if their blood was warm, and why are birds not considered reptiles too if they are a classification of dinosaurs?
Answer: Linnaeus’ taxonomic system was based on morphology - the obvious physical characteristics of animals. For a very long time, that was all we had to go on. So, the designation of reptiles - cold-blooded, scaled animals was obviously distinct from birds - warm-blooded, feathered animals. But now that we are able to sequence genetics, we no longer have to guess about the relationships of living animals from their body structure. We can find out for certain how they are really related. A new system of taxonomy has been devised to represent the relationships of organisms based on their genetics. This allows us to place animals rationally in lines of descent from common ancestors. The system is called cladistics, or phylogenetic taxonomy. A clade is a group that contains a species, and all of that species’ descendants - forever. No skipping from one group to another. No matter how different a descendant is, it remains in that clade. New clades are added as more species differentiate. The only groupings in phylogenetic taxonomy that are not clades are Genera and Species. This is because new species arise frequently, and new genera form from them. While you can bring cladistics all the way down to an individual animal, this is not typically as useful, so species are still referred to by their Genus + species + subspecies name designations. I have explained all of this, because in phylogenetic taxonomy, there is no clade ‘Reptilia.’ Wherever possible, when clades were named, they would use the Linnaean name if it could be applied. But in the case of reptiles… it could not. The ‘Class Reptilia’ is paraphyletic. It doesn’t contain all of its descendants. As you have noted, the Class Reptilia does not contain birds, but they assuredly ARE descendants of the first reptile. As a result, paleontologists virtually NEVER use Linnaean taxonomy. While it still has some use in work on living organisms, it’s a mess of nonsense when you get into extinct life. Paleontologists use phylogenetic taxonomy. And, of course, phylogenetic taxonomy hinges on what you are and where you came from - not what you look like, or what you can do. This is important to understand, because distinctions like whether or not an animal is an endotherm (warm-blooded) or ectotherm (cold-blooded) are irrelevant in phylogenetic taxonomy. The reason this is a more rational way of organizing life becomes clear when you realize that we have now found an endothermic fish. Not a mesotherm - it’s not just partially warm-blooded - it’s fully an endotherm. So, the importance of this characteristic has been overrated. Organisms can evolve endothermy, mesothermy, or ectothermy according to what aids their survival best in their environment, and which mutations happen to occur. This means it’s possible for species that are endotherms to evolve to become ectotherms. And, indeed, there is a hypothesis that crocodilians may have done exactly that. Whether we are able to prove or disprove that remains to be seen, but it is possible. Now, the word ‘reptile’ means an animal that is part of the Class Reptilia - but it’s so embedded in common understanding as referring to Lepidosaurs (tuatara, lizards, and snakes), Testudines (turtles and tortoises), and Crocodilia (crocodiles, caimans, and alligators), that it would be hard to convince people to give it up. Giving it up is a solution - all of these animals are Diapsids, and we could certainly just call them that, instead of ‘reptiles.’ The other solution, that is perhaps easier for people to accept and understand, is just to define ‘reptiles’ not as being members of the Class Reptilia, but instead as members of the Clade Sauropsida (Anapsids and Diapsids). When we say that ‘reptiles’ are synonoymous with ‘Sauropsids,’ then we do say that dinosaurs - and thus, birds - are reptiles. And this is likely the best solution, prior to new generations being trained up without the word reptile being taught to them in school. Keep in mind that we now have evidence that all dinosaurs evolved from a warm-blooded, feathered ancestor. And what’s more, pterosaurs were also warm-blooded, feathered animals, which means that the common ancestor of both, a basal Avemetatarsalian, almost certainly was as well. That is what left open the possibility that endothermy may be a characteristic of Archosaurs, and the crocodilians just re-evolved ectothermy as they became semi-aquatic animals. So, short of evicting Archosauria from the ‘Reptilia,’ what else is there to do? Linnaean taxonomy was already an unholy mess over the whole thing, with Dinosaurs being made a Superorder of reptiles, but birds clearly being dinosaurs, and Aves being a Class… it was and is unworkable. Linnaen taxonomy has passed its time. We cannot use it any longer. It doesn’t make sense. So, in short - birds are dinosaurs, and dinosaurs are reptiles. And that does mean that birds are reptiles. Until such time as we stop using the word ‘reptile.’ Folks who think otherwise are just not up to date, that’s all. (I will add one additional note - in phylogenetic taxonomy, basal amniotes evolved into synapsids, and sauropsids. This means that mammals do not descend from reptiles. They descend from early synapsids, which had some of the same characteristics that early amniotes and early reptiles have, but that isn’t the same thing. So, no, this doesn’t mean that we are reptiles, too).

Name: Donna Fernstrom
Question: What evidence suggests that dinosaurs were more closely related to birds than to reptiles?
Answer: Present evidence makes it clear that birds are just a type of dinosaur. The evidence for this is that all Saurischian dinosaurs have hollow bones. Pterosaurs have been found with down feather impressions as well as dinosaurs, which strongly, strongly suggests that feathers evolved before the dinosaur/pterosaur split - meaning that the very first dinosaur was a feathered animal. The vast array of feathered dinosaur fossils makes it clear now that there isn’t anything particularly unique about birds, as dinosaurs go. If we consider bats to be mammals even though they can fly (which we do), then it would be nonsense to consider birds different from other dinosaurs just because they can fly. Some other dinosaurs are warm-blooded animals with feathers. Some have toothless beaks. Some have pygotyles on their tails. Birds aren’t so special. A better question is, why would anyone think they were anything else at this point? Note: Birds are dinosaurs. Dinosaurs ARE reptiles. Reptiles are not what we used to believe they were. That’s how science goes.

Name: Donna Fernstrom
Question: Does evolution claim that humans' ancestors had tails? If yes, is there an observable example of an animal that lost its tail and its descendants inherited the loss?
Answer: No. Evolution is the name of an observed process by which populations of organisms change genetically and morphologically over time. Processes don’t have opinions or make claims. Evolution isn’t an entity. Evolutionary theory is an explanation of why and how populations of organisms change over time. It also doesn’t include any claims about specific species. Scientists who study the evolution of humans have evidence that the ancestors of humans had tails. No claims necessary there - we have evidence instead of claims. “is there an observable example of an animal that lost its tail and its descendants inherited the loss?” No. That isn’t how evolution through natural selection works, so your second question doesn’t have anything to do with the first one. What you’re describing would be something that would occur in the DISPROVEN theory of Lamarckian Evolution. That theory said that if an individual changed to adapt to its environment, it could pass those changes on to its offspring. For example, if a giraffe routinely stretched its neck up to reach leaves, then its offspring would have longer necks. Or if, as you said, a monkey’s tail was chopped off, its offspring would have no tails. But, as I said, that theory was disproven long ago. That cannot and does not actually happen. The reason that it was in question for a while is interesting, but I won’t bore you with talk of epigenes. What actually happened is that a primate was born with a shorter or missing tail due to a mutation, and it was reproductively successful, so passed the trait on to its offspring. They, in turn, were also successful at reproduction, and passed the trait to their offspring. For whatever reasons, the shorter-tailed/missing tail animals had more offspring than the longer-tailed ones, until eventually the entire population had shorter/missing tails. That’s how evolution through natural selection works. Here is a Manx breed cat, showing that it really just takes one mutation to remove a tail. That isn’t the mutation Great Apes have, of course, since the cat tailless gene is lethal when it’s homozygous. It’s more likely several mutations were involved in the total loss of our tails. But it wasn’t difficult for this to happen in any case, and had nothing to do with chopping off tails.

Name: Donna Fernstrom
Question: Why do evolutionists prefer to pick on the bonobos for comparison with humans, instead of the more intelligent chimpanzees?
Answer: First, there is no such thing as an ‘evolutionist.’ That’s a term that implies that acceptance of settled science is some sort of belief system or that there is some question about evolutionary theory. That is not the case. There are people who accept science, and science-deniers. Science denial is irrational. There is no need for special names for people who accept settled science based on which science they accept. Presumably, if they accept settled science on evolution, they accept settled science on everything else, too. lol. I think part of the issue stems from the fact that in common language, a theory is a speculation - a guess. But scientific terms have different definitions, and the term ‘theory’ in science means ‘an explanation for observed facts which is thoroughly supported by ample evidence, and has no contradictory evidence against it.’ First, a hypothesis is proposed - an explanation for facts we have observed. Then the hypothesis is rigorously tested, and evidence is collected. If the evidence all supports the hypothesis, and none disproves it, then it becomes a theory. Once the body of evidence becomes truly overwhelming and massive, then we say that it is a Proven Theory. Evolutionary theory is a proven theory - it is the closest that science can ever come to producing an absolute truth. There are no remaining doubts about it. Not even one. There is no evidence that does not support it. None at all. So, if you want to question accepted science, then you need to actual do science and research. You need to present material facts that contradict the hypothesis or theory, and they need to have been collected using rational, rigorous methods. You need to actually scientifically DISPROVE a theory in order to effectively overturn it. Anything else is meaningless nonsense; irrational behavior based in pretending that reality is not what it is. And no, believing someone else who said they did the work is not sufficient. You have to actually explore and understand their work, and it has to have been duplicated and verified. No one takes anyone at their word. Belief should never have a role to play in any of this. Science is about using a rational method to explore reality and find out what it really is. It does not include faith/absolute certainty, ever. I wanted to make this clear before moving on to the next part of your question, because you went on to state a couple more things that weren’t true. First you said that scientists (this is what you really meant) choose to compare humans and bonobos rather than humans and chimps. This is simply not true. Both species are compared to humans, and their cognition is studied to aid our understanding of our own evolution. Next, you said that chimpanzees are more intelligent than bonobos. This is also not true. Intelligence is not all one thing, and these two species have different intellectual strengths and weaknesses from each other, as well as from us. Bonobos are far more skilled at solving tasks that relate to the theory of mind and social causality, while chimps are more skilled at solving tasks that relate to tool use and physical causality. In short, bonobos are better at knowing themselves and others, while chimps are better at understanding physics. Chimpanzees are far more aggressive than bonobos, and this holds them back to some degree. They are, in fact, more aggressive than humans, having a significantly higher rate of reactive aggression. Bonobos, conversely, are about equal to humans in reactive aggression. Chimps also have a higher rate of proactive aggression than humans do, but humans have a higher rate of proactive aggression than Bonobos. To put this into perspective, a chimp is smart enough to sharpen a stick to stab you with because you made him angry by grinning at him. And he’ll do it, too. lol. A bonobo is smart enough to understand that you aren’t a bonobo and your body language is different from his, so he doesn’t have any reason to be angry that you grinned at him. Which one is ‘smarter?’ I will also leave you with the fact that humans are not superior in all areas of cognition to our closest relatives. As I pointed out, cognition is not all one thing. And we don’t win in every area. Chimpanzees wipe the floor with us in tests of working memory. No contest. Even when we have time to practice, they still beat us. They are simply BETTER at noting where things are, exactly, and remembering it five minutes later when they can’t see those things anymore. As for bonobos - a bonobo was able to recognize both her sister and her nephew in photographs after not having seen either one for 26 years, which is the longest term social memory documented in a non-human animal. (I don’t think the working memory of bonobos has been tested, yet). So, we have very good reasons to study the cognitive abilities of both species, as an aid to understanding how various parts of the brain work, and how our own cognitive arrangement likely evolved.

Question: Is it possible for any creatures to reach the size of dinosaurs after their extinction? Is there a specific reason why no other creatures have evolved to be as large as dinosaurs?
Answer: Sure, it’s possible. The Earth’s biosphere is always changing, and we’ve destroyed entire ecosystems, devastated others, and changed the climate, triggering a mass extinction event. Huge animals need a lot of food. Unless we stop destroying literally everything, there won’t be enough food to support the evolution of a huge animal. If we actually stop destroying rainforests and let the Earth’s ecosystems recover, and leave space for wild creatures, eventually a land animal that large could evolve again. And if it does, it will probably be a dinosaur. Because dinosaurs didn’t all become extinct - we still have avian dinosaurs, which means the potential of the dinosaurian lineage is still right there in them. The reason I say that it’s more likely that a bird will evolve into an enormous animal is because Saurischian dinosaur bones are made of very dense, strong material, and they are also hollow and full of air, connected to the respiratory system. That’s what allowed the sauropod dinosaurs to reach such gargantuan sizes. The very largest sauropods show signs of stress fractures in their bones - a result of just living and moving at that tremendous size and weight. They’re at the limit of what’s possible for a land animal with a bone skeleton, and it’s all due to the clever latticework inside their hollow, lightweight bones. The bones of a Saurischian dinosaur are much stronger than a mammal bone of the same size, but weigh about the same. Birds are saurischian dinosaurs. A land mammal could never reach the size of a sauropod dinosaur, because their bones would have to be too large and heavy for it to be feasible. If they evolved denser bones, and hollow bones, they could do it - but that’s a much longer and far less likely evolutionary path than a bird simply evolving into a huge animal. It would be easier for a bird to evolve into a giant quadruped than for a mammal to evolve Saurischian dinosaur-like bones. Of course, dinosaurs ranged in size from the tiny Bee Hummingbird on up to the largest sauropods, and everything in between. Prior to the K-Pg extinction, there were plenty of small non-avian dinosaurs as well. So, ‘as large as dinosaurs’ depends on which dinosaurs you mean. There were quite a few rather large dinosaurs, but there have also been some rather large mammals. Tyrannosaurus rex on the left, Paraceratherium, an extinct relative of the rhinoceros, on the right. Mammals may not be able to become as large as a sauropod, but they can become as large as a Tyrannosaur or Triceratops. And at least one did. It became extinct 23 million years ago. And the crown of ‘largest confirmed animal to have ever lived’ still sits on the head of the Blue Whale, endangered but hanging in there, alive today. With the sea supporting its weight, it doesn’t have to worry about issues with bone strength and size.

Question: Is the belief that birds evolved from dinosaurs still held by paleoartists? Can you provide examples of this belief being depicted in artworks?
Answer: Kind of, but really it’s the wrong way to put it, as it’s now clear that birds are dinosaurs. When you say something ‘evolved from’ something else, it sort of implies that it has stopped being the former thing when it became the new thing. Birds never stopped being dinosaurs. This became clear when we found the gorgeous fossils in China that show many theropod dinosaurs had feathers. This spurred researchers to look harder for feather traces in other dinosaur fossils, and they found quite a few of them. Feather were typical in theropods, though some lineages didn’t have them (Carnotaurus, for example, doesn’t have any feathers associated with it - neither does Tyrannosaurus rex, although its cousin, Yutyrannus huali, was very feathered and very fluffy). We’ve now found down feathers on a pterosaur, which strongly implies that feathers evolved before the split between dinosaurs and pterosaurs, since both have them. And if that’s so, that means that the common ancestor of dinosaurs and pterosaurs must have been a warm-blooded, feathered animal. Which also means the very first dinosaur (possibly Nyasasaurus) would have been warm-blooded and feathered. (By Scott Reid on @drawingwithdinosaurs) So, as you can see, the first dinosaur doesn’t look all that different from a bird in many ways. Well… more accurately, we would say that birds still look pretty similar to the first dinosaurs. Far from being a ‘belief,’ this is a scientifically supported theory. (A theory in science is not a guess, but is an explanation for facts which has substantial scientific evidence supporting it, and no evidence against it). It is accepted because science supports it as being true. Unlike a belief, if some evidence against it comes to light (very unlikely at this point), then it will be discarded. One of the earliest Avialans (Anchiornis huxleyi, in real colors determined from traces in the fossil). (Image: Zhao Chuang; courtesy of Peking Natural Science Organization) Some define ‘birds’ as being members of the clade Avialae - in which case, Archaeopteryx is a bird, possibly the first bird. (by Vaderxl ) Others define ‘birds’ as being specifically members of the clade Aves/Neornithes, in which case the first bird might be Gallornis. (By Scott Reid on @drawingwithdinosaurs) To put this debate into perspective, the picture below is an Avialan, but not a Neornithine. This animal is part of a group of Avialans called Enantiornithes, which were the most diverse and common of the avialans at the time that the Chicxulub asteroid struck. Art by: Enantiornithes were different from modern birds in that they hatched out with fully developed wings, and it’s believed that they were able to fly within days, possibly hours after hatching. It’s likely that their parents provided no parental care for them, but that they were on their own from the start. (This is rare in modern birds, but Kiwis also provide no parental care for their chicks once they hatch - their only concession is to allow the chicks to remain in their territory until mature). As you can see, though, enantiornithes certainly look like what we think of as a bird. No enantiornithes survived the K-Pg Extinction. Your question suggests that you may be unaware of how far we have come, and how much evidence we now have about theropod dinosaurs and bird evolution. Hopefully you have found this enlightening. :)

Question: Can individuals with autism develop empathy? What factors may influence this development?
Answer: Empathy is the ability to mirror another person’s emotions - to feel what they are feeling, so you understand it from the inside. Individuals with autism typically have a high level of empathy, in some cases even excessive empathy. But, since they are not necessarily psychic, their empathy relies on the same cues that most people’s empathy relies on. Tone of voice, body language, facial expressions… you know, all of the things that persons with autism are absolutely terrible at interpreting. But if you tell an autistic person that you’re extremely sad, and why, they’ll feel for you as much or more as anyone else, possibly to an uncomfortable degree. We’re just not as likely to know how you are feeling if you don’t tell us, because we are poor at interpreting your facial expressions, tone of voice, and body language. This is the reason why persons with autism were initially believed to lack empathy - if you don’t know a person is sad, you can’t feel sad along with them. So, people would be emoting, and we wouldn’t react, because we didn’t know what they were emoting, you see. But, no - nothing wrong with our empathy at all.

Question: My sister's 10 year old son has autism really bad and nobody really likes him. The kid is a total nightmare. How do I politely exclude her from an upcoming family gathering?
Answer: If he’s a total nightmare, he is almost certainly IN a living nightmare. He would probably not enjoy the family gathering. It would probably be best to allow him to decide if he wants to go, and be prepared to leave if he is overwhelmed. If he is not capable of communication, then she should certainly not bring him to such a chaotic gathering. He would be miserable. That doesn’t mean she can’t go, but she would need a carer for him. As someone with autism, your wanting to include us is very nice, but we aren’t going to want to be there if it’s going to overwhelm us. Your wanting to exclude the child because you don’t like him is unfair. Instead, consider it from his point of view. Remember that persons with autism have meltdowns because they are overwhelmed. To get some idea of what this is like, imagine being in a room with five guys dancing around you. One is banging pots, one is randomly spraying you with water, one is poking you with the bristles of a hairbrush in random places, one is asking you questions and demanding answers, and the last one is flashing lights in your eyes. Now, put up with this indefinitely while you try to go through your everyday life. How long would it take before you lashed out? If any little thing broke your concentration, wouldn’t you pretty much lose it? Because you can never get rid of those five guys. It’s not an exact analogy, but this is PRETTY MUCH what severe autism is like. And routine and focus on the things they like helps them tune out the five guys. Things which break that focus mean that the five guys become more obvious, and their torment becomes harder to ignore, until they snap. Who wouldn’t? Suggest to your sister that her son probably wouldn’t enjoy the gathering, or if he does want to go, would want to leave very soon after arriving, and ask if she wants to attend and has a caregiver lined up for him. Frankly, if she does not understand all of this, she’s not doing a great job of parenting someone with autism.

Question: Is it possible for chimpanzees to evolve into humans or another type of ape/monkey species, considering they are our closest relative on earth?

It isn’t possible for the same exact mutations to all occur and all be reinforced in the same exact ways. So, no - neither chimps, nor any other primate, can evolve into humans. They could evolve into a sophont species, but they cannot evolve, specifically, into humans. The common ancestor of chimps and humans is extinct. When it is said that extinction is forever, that is a truth. Once gone, it can never evolve again. It’s gone forever.

Question: The minute that wolves evolved into dogs, supposing that no more wolves exited after that, would that mean wolves are now extinct?

(Most likely, humans did not deliberately selectively breed them, but they did encourage the less aggressive and more useful dogs, and discouraged or killed the aggressive, unhelpful ones. They would even have allowed the cute, kind dogs to have scraps and more food, which made them more successful at surviving and breeding). Dogs were domesticated quite a long time before humans adopted agriculture, so the notion of selective breeding likely wasn’t a thing back then. The subspecies of wolves that dogs evolved from is extinct - or possibly pseudo-extinct (meaning that the entire population of that subspecies evolved into dogs). There are many subspecies of gray wolves, though. The other subspecies didn’t have anything to do with dogs (for the most part). That’s why there are still plenty of gray wolves today. There are three species of wolves (gray wolves, red wolves, and timber wolves), and possibly as many as 40 different subspecies. Domestic dogs represent only one subspecies. It’s possibly you meant your question as just an example, however, as obviously you know that gray wolves are not extinct. If that is so, then the term you are looking for is ‘pseudo-extinct.’ That it what it would be called when the entire population of a species becomes another species via evolution. (For example, Homo heidelbergensis in Africa became pseudo-extinct when they evolved into Homo sapiens).

Question: Why don't fruit bats and vampire bats die of rabies? "Perhaps, the most heretical disclosure was that vampire bats could recover from the furious stage of the disease and were capable of spreading the disease up to five and one half months.”

Surely if the animal is recovered, it would not show up, either. Vampire bats seem less likely to display furious rabies to begin with, but they do behave normally for some time while infectious, prior to declining and dying. Male bats tend to be aggressive anyhow, but if anything, their aggression levels often decrease if they contract rabies. (This is not to say vampire bats never display furious rabies, just that it’s less common). Vampire bats have evolve resistance to the rabies virus because their diet puts them in contact with it so frequently. Perhaps fruit bats of some species have also evolved resistance. Colonial bats in general seem to be less prone to displaying furious rabies (instead, displaying paralytic rabies symptoms). Typically, rabies kills the bats it infects, and entire vampire bat colonies have been destroyed by the virus, leaving too few living animals to support the colony. A dose of the virus that would be sufficient to infect 50% of dogs exposed will only infect 10% of vampire bats exposed, so their resistance is quite high. Bats also carry a number of Lyssaviruses other than Rabies virus itself. There’s a lot we still don’t understand about rabies in bats, especially vampire bats. A program to try culling the bats to reduce a rabies epidemic oddly made things worse instead.

Question: Did dinosaurs have a similar nesting behavior to modern birds, or did they have other methods of protecting their eggs and hatchlings?

Birds have more diverse nesting behaviors than most people realize. This is a brush turkey. It lives in Australia, and it nests in a similar fashion to an alligator. It’s built that big mound of moist, rotting vegetation. Its eggs are buried in there, using the heat of the decaying vegetation to keep them warm. The bird guards the mound and adds or subtracts vegetation to control the temperature, just as alligators do with their mound nests. Some dinosaurs buried their eggs in sand or soil and left them, as turtles do. Some would create mounds like this to incubate their eggs, and guard them. Some would sit on their eggs, as most birds do. Some young dinosaurs were on their own from the moment they hatched, some were looked after by their parents, and some stayed in the nest and were fed by their parents. Modern birds use all three tactics.

Question: Is there a relationship between dinosaurs and birds? Could this potentially lead to the resurrection of extinct dinosaur species in the future?
Answer: It’s the same as the relationship between mammals and humans. Birds are dinosaurs. No, we won’t be resurrecting any extinct dinosaur species. The reason we won’t be doing that is that the DNA that made them unique species has been lost. It doesn’t exist any longer. And while we might get the occasional snippet of protein from fossils, DNA is fragile, and we will never be able to find enough to restore even a single complete gene from a non-avian dinosaur species. Their genomes are gone forever. What we could potentially do is use genetic engineering to create something similar using bird DNA as a base. But that, too, is a long way off. Cloning and genetically engineering animal that reproduce via amniote eggs isn’t something we’ve managed to solve yet, just for starters. Because of the way eggs form, it’s a horrifically difficult problem. With placental mammals, you can just inject some hormones and pop the embryo into the uterus, and a lot of times it will embed and grow. But the embyro of an egg-laying animal has to actually be embedded at the exact right stage of development while the egg is forming! You can’t take an infertile egg and put an embryo in it, it doesn’t work. So far, we’ve been able to create only the simplest organism using a printed DNA genome and a cell that has been emptied of its DNA. So it’s going to be a long while before we understand DNA and the proteome well enough to create a complex life form, much less tailor one to look and behave the way we want it to.

Question: Were mammals or reptiles (including birds) more closely related to dinosaurs?

Clade Dinosauria is within Clade Diapsida, while Clade Mammalia is within in Clade Synapsida. Clade Diapsida and Clade Anapsida are within Clade Sauropsida. Clade Synapsida is by itself. Synapsida and Sauropsida diverged shortly after the first Amniotes evolved. Linnaean taxonomy is passe` and is increasingly disused. Phylogenetic taxonomy (cladistics) is tremendously more accurate and practically useful. People who study extinct organisms pretty much never use Linnaean taxonomy now. Insofar as ‘reptile’ means anything anymore, it’s used as a synonym for Sauropsid. Birds are dinosaurs. Dinosaurs are reptiles. Mammals are not reptiles and are not descended from reptiles.

Question: Is it true that birds are considered to be small living dinosaurs? If so, why have they not gone extinct like their larger relatives?

The vast, vast majority of birds did not survive the Chicxulub disaster. The largest clade of birds alive at that time, the Enantiornithes, all perished. The bird species that did survive were all modestly-sized ground-nesting birds. (Trees would have perished in droves - to regrow from nuts and seeds later after the clouds dispersed and the weather warmed again). The Chicxulub impact destroyed 80% of all species on Earth at that time, both on land and in the sea. Only a few species of avian dinosaurs lived - and a few species of mammals. (Most mammals alive then also died). All modern mammals and birds descended from those few surviving species.

Question: Is it possible for a dog with no visible signs of rabies to still carry and transmit the disease to humans or other animals? If so, what are the chances of this occurring?

Rabies can incubate for weeks, months, or in a few rare cases, even years - but an animal incubating rabies is not infectious. It can only pass the virus once the disease becomes ACTIVE - a day before, and during, the time that it shows actual symptoms.

Question: What is the difference between an alpha wolf and a regular wolf? Why do people say "alpha wolf" instead of just "wolf"?
Answer: A regular wolf is a real wolf in the real world. An ‘alpha wolf’ is a made-up idea that came about due to researchers studying wolves kept in captivity that were forced into unnatural social groups, and had to make do and figure out how to get along. People say ‘alpha wolf’ because they don’t know any better, and still believe wolf packs are led by a single dominant individual that bosses all the other wolves around, and uses aggression and strength to keep them in line. A regular wolf, on the other hand, finds a mate, and the pair then stakes out a territory away from other wolves, and they start a family. The pack is made of the breeding pair and their offspring. As the young grow to adulthood, some stay with the pack to help raise their younger siblings, while some strike out on their own to find mates of their own. The parents are the leaders of the pack, of course, because parents always lead their children. They switch off duties - sometimes mom is mostly in charge, and sometimes dad is. The kids bicker among themselves, work out a pecking order, and engage in a bit of bullying, the way kids are prone to do. Mom and dad mostly keep them in line.

Question: From what I understand, the alpha male and female are the only ones that mate in a wolf pack. How does this affect the social structure of the pack?

That stuff came from observing stressed-out captive wolves that had been forced to live together with others not of their choosing, and had to make do somehow. In the wild, a wolf pack is a family. That’s all it is, nothing more. You have mom, dad, and the kids. Sometimes you’ve got mom or dad’s brother or sister, but usually not. Just a family. The pack is just the grown kids of the mated pair, helping look after and raise their younger siblings. Eventually, many of them will leave the pack and go wandering, hoping to entice another young adult away from another pack, or find another wandering adult looking to strike out on their own. If they do, and they like them, they’ll pair up, find a territory of their own, and start a new pack. (Lone wolf is only ever meant to be a temporary situation). The mated pair are in charge because they’re the parents of the others. They’re the only ones that mate because the rest of them are all siblings, so you sure don’t want to let them have pups with each other, lol. (And mostly they’re not inclined to anyhow).

Question: How can I heat up my snake tank? I have a ball python and the power just went out and its 34 degrees outside. I fed him this morning and would rather not move his whole enclosure. Do I have any options to keep him warm?
Answer: This is an emergency situation. Your ball python should not be exposed to temperatures under 70F at all, and temperatures under 60F are EXTREMELY dangerous. Remove the ball python from its enclosure, and tie it in a pillow case. You can warm up your car and keep the snake warm there until you have the supplies you need. If you have an insulated box used for shipping reptiles, put the snake in it with a hand warmer. Wrap the hand warmer carefully in a thick towel so the snake cannot be burned. (Hand warmers typically get too hot for any sort of direct contact). You can also use a cooler, just open the water vent hole to let fresh air in, or punch a small hole in the side with a pencil if it is styrofoam. (You don’t need more than one hole - snakes require much less oxygen than a bird or mammal, and more holes would compromise the insulation). Use an indoor/outdoor thermometer with a probe to keep track of the temperature inside of the cooler or box. It’s important that it never falls below 70F or above 90F. For the future, buy an insulated reptile shipping box the right size for your snake. Keep it, a pillowcase or snake bag, and a supply of two or three 40 hour reptile shipping heat packs (you can buy them online). The 24 hour kind aren’t as safe (they spike hotter), so get the 40 hour at minimum. That way, if the power goes out, you will have the right supplies on hand to keep your snake safe. A snake can be kept in a shipping box for up to two days if necessary. After that, you will need to give the opportunity to drink water. If your snake has been exposed to temperatures under 70F, observe it VERY carefully for the next week for symptoms of respiratory infection. If you see the snake sitting with its head angled up or mouth open, see bubbly spit in its mouth, or hear it rasp (or feel a rattle when holding it when it breathes) take it to a reptile vet immediately. (Respiratory infections can generally be easily treated with a course of antibiotics if caught early, but are likely to prove deadly if not treated).

Question: How long can a ball python stay in its cage without needing to be misted or fed?
Answer: Ball pythons don’t need to be ‘misted’ at all. They shouldn’t be wet unless they decide to climb into their water bowl and soak. Keep the enclosure at 80F with a 90F basking spot at all times. Use a solid-top reptile cage, not an aquarium with a screen top. The humidity in the enclosure should ALWAYS be between 60% and 80%. The substrate should be dry. Under-cage heating controlled by a digital thermostat is necessary (the thermostat is not optional). Heat lamps are not advised - they dry the cage too much, and are a fire hazard. Fresh, clean water must be available at all times. Place the water bowl over the under-cage heat source if you need to raise the humidity. Misting isn’t the way to go. How long a ball python can go without a meal depends on its age and condition. A fat, healthy adult ball python could go 8 to 12 months without food. A really young hatchling cannot - they might go a month, but shouldn’t go longer. And that only if they’ve got decent weight to start with. But it is recommended that adult ball pythons be fed once per week, or once every two weeks. (Sizes of these animals adults can vary substantially, with some being twice as large as others, so that makes a difference in how much food they need). Male ball pythons frequently fast for 3 months over the winter (this varies between individuals, though).

Question: Why did stegosaurs go extinct before the other dinosaurs, right in the middle of the Cretaceous?
Answer: Well, for starters, we’re not entirely certain that they did. It’s possible that one or a few species may have survived right up until K-Pg. It’s also possible that they died out right at the beginning of the Cretaceous. Further study of existing fossils is needed to verify these things. (We have some possible fossils from Russia which might be Stegosaurs from the middle of the Cretaceous, and also a fossil from India which might be one, from near K-Pg, but those things need to be verified, as the fossils are very incomplete and the identity isn’t yet certain). The evidence suggests that there was a severe decline in species starting just before the beginning of the Cretaceous, and climate change and the evolution of some predatory dinosaurs that may have been better at killing it might in combination be responsible. So, if Stegosaurus (which is a genus, not a single species) did indeed not make it to K-Pg, climate/environmental change is the most likely reason why not. Specifically, Stegosaurus were specialized cycad eaters, and cycads began dwindling due to intense competition from angiosperms at the beginning of the Cretaceous. There are a few cycad species still alive today, but cycads are not numerous. Stegosaurus were large animals that required a lot of food. With the larger cycads becoming extinct and their distribution sparser, it would have been a challenge for them to feed themselves. This would explain why, if they did survive, they became far less numerous (not only in species, but in total numbers). Fossilization is rare, so an uncommon species is much less likely to fossilize, too.

Question: Have scientists always known that chickens are not closely related to dinosaurs, or were they ever considered descendants due to similarities with modern day birds?

Birds are, unquestionably, by every definition, straight-up dinosaurs. They are part of clade Dinosauria. Birds are Maniraptoran Theropod Dinosaurs. With this revelation, it became clear that birds aren’t special at all. They’re just typical dinosaurs, adapted for flight, sure, but no more different from other dinosaurs than a bat or dolphin is different from other mammals. Next, chickens. Chickens are birds. Birds, clade Avialae, first evolved around 165 million years ago. Around 66 million years ago, a massive asteroid struck the Earth near the tip of the Yucatan Peninsula, and wiped out 80% of all species on Earth. It eradicated all of the marine reptiles, all of the pterosaurs, and most of the dinosaurs (including all of the non-avian dinosaurs, and most of the avians). Only a few species in a few clades of avian dinosaurs survived. Among them were the Paleognaths and Neognaths. Among the surviving Neognaths were Neoaves and Galloanserae (ducks and chickens are part of this clade). Perhaps you were confused by the fact that chickens descend from a lineage of birds that split from other bird lineages before the mass extinction event. But chickens are, of course, still birds. And birds are dinosaurs, so chickens are dinosaurs.

Question: Is there a reason why dinosaurs did not evolve into mammals instead of reptiles?
Answer: Nothing evolves into the same thing twice. Evolution is a complex process involving random mutations and selective pressures. The first amniotes, animals that had a membrane inside their eggs to keep them from drying out on land, diverged into two primary lineages: The Synapsids and the Sauropsids. Mammals are Synapsids. Dinosaurs are Sauropsids. Mammals evolved only about 5 million years after the first dinosaurs evolved, but their lineages had been separate at that point for at least 100 million years. We now understand that mammals never evolved from reptiles. The reptile line are the Sauropsids, you see. Both reptiles (sauropsids) and synapsids (mammals are synapsids) evolved from basal amniotes. The only reason you don’t hear the word ‘synapsid’ very often is because mammals are the only synapsids left alive. The synapsids didn’t have the robust diversity that reptiles have. In the reptiles, you have Lepidosaurs (lizards, snakes, and tuataras remain), Testudines (turtles and tortoises remain), and Archosaurs (crocodilians and dinosaurs remain - yes, birds are dinosaurs). In the synapsids, it’s only Mammalia remaining, and only monotremes, marsupials and placentals. So, the reason that dinosaurs did not evolve into mammals is because mammals are from a lineage that split away from the dinosaur line a very long time before there were any dinosaurs around, and are radically different from them. On the other hand, you can take some joy in knowing that dinosaurs still exist. They didn’t all die during the asteroid strike. It turns out that birds aren’t just descended from dinosaurs - they actually are dinosaurs, after all.

Question: What are the differences between wild dogs and wolves? Can both be domesticated if raised from pups?
Answer: The term ‘wild dog’ is ambiguous. It may refer to any wild canine, including wolves. It might refer to a specific species of wild dog, such as the Dhole or the African Painted Hunting Dog. It might refer to feral domesticated dogs. If you had something specific in mind, you should name the species in your question. You cannot domesticate an individual animal. You can only tame it. A tame wild animal is still a wild animal. Likewise, a feral domesticated animal is still a domesticated animal. Domestication is genetic. It means the population has been selectively bred by humans to better suit a human purpose for enough generations that it is substantially different from wild populations of the species. Any animal can be tamed if raised from infancy and carefully worked with. How trustworthy it is at that point depends on the species, and on the individual. In most cases, a tame wild animal isn’t trustworthy because it is higher strung and much more reactive as a result of evolutionary selection for survival in the wild. If you take in feral domestic dog puppies, and raise them by hand, you wind up with just ordinary dogs. There’s nothing special about their mother being feral. Their genetics are the same as any other domestic dog. If you hand raise a wolf pup or a dhole pup, you wind up with tame captive wildlife. In short, only part of your question can be answered as as you asked it, because your question is too ambiguous for a more thorough answer.

Question: Do you think that dinosaurs had feathers before birds existed? If so, when did they lose their feathers (if at all)?
Answer: Recently, we’ve found true down feathers on a pterosaur. This puts to rest the idea that pycnofibers evolved separately from protofeathers. The pycnofibers are protofeathers, and this means that the origin of protofeathers is pushed back to before the split between the pterosaur and dinosaur lineages, in the Avemetatarsalians that gave rise to both of them. Both dinosaurs and pterosaurs had feathers. This means that the first dinosaur had feathers (protofeathers, probably - single hollow fibers, or possibly primitive down feathers). It must have, or no dinosaurs that came after could have had them. So, feathers are completely typical for dinosaurs. It’s clear some dinosaurs lost their feathers, but many kept them, and the feathers continued to evolve. All dinosaurs also had scales (birds do, too, on their feet and sometimes legs). In some dinosaur lineages, they simply evolved to have more scales and fewer feathers until no feathers were left. They often had decorative bristles, though - feather shafts. We have evidence of feathers on dinosaur fossils from both the Ornithischian and Saurischian lineages (birds are Saurischians). They’re much more common in Saurischians. Some of the largest Saurischian predators didn’t seem to have them - Carnotaurus probably didn’t, and Tyrannosaurus rex probably didn’t, but Yutyrannus definitely did, as did most of the others (Therizinosaurs, troodons, dromaeosaurs, etc etc). So, dinosaurs definitely had feathers before the Avialae line (birds) evolved, and many of them kept their feathers, while some lost them. We don’t know exactly when some dinosaur lineages lost their feathers, and even in cases where we have scaled skin impressions, we can’t rule out the dinosaurs having quills or feathers somewhere else on their body. Fossils like the incredible Nodosaur fossil found which is like 1/3 of the animal, are astoundingly rare.

Question: How did dinosaurs evolve into birds? Was it through micro-evolution or macro-evolution?
Answer: There is no such thing as ‘micro’ or ‘macro’ evolution. Evolution through natural selection is all there is. It’s one thing. It refers to changes in a population of organisms over time. Evolution can occur slowly or more rapidly, depending on the organism’s resistance to mutation, reproductive rate, and the strength of selective forces. By the time the first birds evolved, the clade of dinosaurs they descended from already looked like this: ( Jianianhualong tengi by Julius T. Csotonyi) Many maniraptoran dinosaurs had similar appearances. This is a reconstruction of the actual Velociraptor mongoliensis (yes, the movie lied). ( © Fred Wierum, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons) Some dromaeosaurs (raptors) could probably glide or even fly short distances. Microraptor, famously four-winged (with lift-providing feathers on its hind legs as well as forelegs), for example. By the time the first true member of the Avialae evolved, there were a LOT of other dinosaurs around that looked very much like it, but were not birds. Birds really aren’t unusual as dinosaurs go - they don’t have very many unique features. We used to think they were very different, but we were mistaken. It turns out that a bird is really quite a typical dinosaur, and no more different from other dinosaurs than a bat is different from other mammals. Even less so, in many ways. I’ve detailed this because it’s very important to understand that punctuated equilibrium occurs in little baby steps, not huge jumps. Crocodiles don’t suddenly stand up on two legs in a couple of generations. Noticeable evolutionary transitions are small, and for vertebrates like these, take more than a hundred years at the quickest, and tens of thousands at the slowest. Evolution is only instant and dramatic when it occurs as a result of hybridization.

Question: What is the difference between dinosaurs and reptiles? Why are dinosaurs called dinosaurs if they're not reptiles and their names end with "saurus" (meaning lizard in Latin)?
Answer: The real answer to this question is that it is a quirk of Taxonomy. Scientific nomenclature was developed so that scientists across the entire world could have a common language to use to discuss living things. Common names can be wildly different between countries, and in some cases the same name can refer to several different species. So it was necessary to come up with names that apply to only one species, everywhere, regardless of the language you speak. The entire taxonomic tree is created this way. A dinosaur is a dinosaur in every language on Earth! A Chinese scientists calls them dinosaurs, and so do American, German, and Brazilian scientists. But the person who first proposes/discovers a clade and has it accepted is the one who gets to name it. And once it is named, that name will NEVER be changed unless the clade/taxonomic group is changed. When dinosaur fossils were first discovered, scientists thought they looked like giant lizards, so the taxonomic name created was ‘Thunder Lizards.’ We know now that they’re not anything like lizards at all, but the taxonomic group was correctly constructed - it’s a Superorder in Linnaean Taxonomy, and a Clade in Phylogenetic taxonomy, and it did not need to be reconstructed, so the name remains! But the same is not true of the term ‘reptile.’ In phylogenetic taxonomy, there is no clade ‘Reptilia,’ because the Class Reptilia in Linnaean taxonomy was proven to be paraphyletic (it didn’t contain all of its descendants). That’s a no-no in phylogenetic taxonomy. Clades consist of a species and all of its descendant species. So, now, the new name is Sauropsida. As Linnaean taxonomy ceases to be used, the word reptile will no longer be a scientific word. So, in phylogenetic taxonomy, Dinosaurs are not reptiles because there is no such thing as a reptile. They are Sauropsids. But the terms are considered to be pretty much synonymous at this time. So it’s still okay to say that Dinosaurs are reptiles. In Linnaean taxonomy, Dinosaurs are reptiles. Since birds are dinosaurs, this means that birds are reptiles. Isn’t taxonomy fun?

For example, tigers and lions. (Panthera tigris and Panthera leo). In some cases, they can produce offspring, but the offspring are usually sterile. For example, horses and donkeys. Equus caballus and Equus asinus). And sometimes, species within the same genus cannot hybridize at all. But often, when this happens, taxonomists will choose to assign the completely genetically incompatible species to a new genus. To make matters even more complex, sometimes members of different genera can interbreed as well. And all of the aforementioned options apply to inter-generic hybrids. Often, they are fully fertile. For example, corn snakes and kingsnakes. (Pantherophis guttatus and Lampropeltis getula). Rarest of all, sometimes members of different clades can interbreed successfully! Question: Are the Na’vis classified as mammals?
Answer: No. Mammalia is a Class/Clade in Terrestrial taxonomy. A clade, by definition, consists of an organism and all of its descendants. The Na’vi do not descend from the first mammal, therefore they are not mammals. No extraterrestrial falls into any of the classifications we use for Earth life. There are no extraterrestrial animals, plants, or fungi. They did not descend from our LUCA. They don’t fall into Domain Archaea, Bacteria, or Eukaryota. They descend from a different last universal common ancestor entirely, and their taxonomic tree would therefore be completely different. Even if they were to look exactly like us (so tremendously unlikely), they would be less closely related to us than we are to the most bizarre and different bacterium that has ever existed. They’re less closely related to us than we are to any of our viruses.

Question: What is the difference between macroevolution and microevolution? What is the difference between common descent and punctuated equilibrium?
Answer: There’s no such thing as ‘macroevolution’ or ‘microevolution.’ It’s all just evolution. Those terms are only used by science deniers who don’t understand evolution. Common descent refers to species which have diverged, but have a common ancestor. For example, the last common ancestor of chimps and humans diverged into at least two species - one that led to chimps, and one that led to humans. So, we share common descent with chimps. Punctuated equilibrium refers to the fact that reinforcing selection occurs in a population of organisms when their environment is relatively stable, and they’re well-adapted to it. They tend to stay roughly the same in morphology over time. Once the environment changes, however, they may rapidly evolve changes to cope with their new environment, and then, once the environment stabilizes in its new configuration, they will stabilize again. So, they maintain equilibrium (not changing very much) when conditions stay the same, with punctuation (rapid change) when conditions change. Conditions are changing rapidly right now, so we’re going to start seeing some interesting rapid evolution, along with the mass extinction. Anything that cannot evolve quickly enough to cope will become extinct.

Question: If we evolved from chimpanzees, why don’t the in-between stages of the evolution still exist?
Answer: We did not evolve from chimpanzees. Chimpanzees and humans both evolved from a common ancestor via a process called ‘divergent evolution.’ This occurs when a population of a species gets separated from the rest, either by learned behavior, or a physical/geographic barrier. As a result of that separation, they no longer breed with members of the original population (or at lest, very rarely). This allows the two populations to evolve separately in different directions. As time passes, they become less and less alike. The reason ‘in-between stages’ don’t exist is because all evolution results in one of two outcomes - extinction, in which all members of the species/population have died and left no offspring, or pseudo-extinction, in which all members of the population have substantially changed over time enough that none of them fit the definition of the original species any longer, and all are considered to be a new species. Hybridization also plays a role in evolution, where a breeding with a closely related (or perhaps not so closely related) species can bring different genes into the population en masse. A successful hybrid can sow new, useful genes into the population it’s a member of, or can even found a new species entirely (if it has enough hybrid siblings). The course of human evolution has involved both extinctions and pseudo-extinctions. Our immediate ancestor is pseudo-extinct. All other species of humans that diverged from that lineage along the way are extinct. We carry hybrid genes from at least three of them. The truth is, evolution, being a blind process, produces a lot of failures. Mostly failures, really. The vast majority of species on Earth have become extinct, not pseudo-extinct. You will notice that this particular graph just shows the time periods these species lived in, and doesn’t have any lines showing descent. Descent is REALLY difficult to figure out when you have so many closely-related species, and so much evidence that they hybridized. We do know that Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthals) were not our ancestors. They were a sibling species, descended from the same common ancestor. Their differences were the result of divergent evolution. We suspect our immediate ancestor (and that of Neanderthals) was Homo heidelbergensis, or possibly a species called Homo antecessor. Possibly something like this: Forensic reconstruction of Homo heidelbergensis and Homo antecessor, our two most probable ancestors: As you can see, while they look a bit unusual, they don’t look so strange that if you dressed them up in a suit and passed them on the street, you would actually notice them overly much. Evolution is a gradual process, and a new species doesn’t look all THAT much different from the one it evolved from. For fun, here is Homo neanderthalensis, our sibling species, wearing a suit. (This is a meticulously reconstructed wax figure currently residing in a German museum): We hybridized with this species, and most of us have some Neanderthal genes. Up to 4% in some people.

Question: What is the difference between dinosaurs and birds? Do both have feathers? Do both walk on two feet? Why did dinosaurs become extinct?
Answer: This question is similar to asking ‘what is the difference between fruits and apples?’ It doesn’t really make sense because it’s based on an incorrect premise. That premise is that birds are something different from dinosaurs. But that isn’t true. Birds are just one branch of dinosaurs, the same way that bats are one branch of mammals. We used to think that dinosaurs were primitive reptiles, and that birds evolved from them, but were substantially different. In the past decade or two, that has been proven to be entirely wrong. We started finding tons of dinosaur fossils with feathers. Then, more recently, a particularly important discovery was made. True down feathers were found on a pterosaur. Pterosaurs are not dinosaurs - but they evolved from a common ancestor. The presence of feathers on a pterosaur strongly, strongly implies that feathers evolved before there even WERE dinosaurs. That the Avemetatarsalians that gave rise to both clades, dinosaur and pterosaur, had already evolved protofeathers. And that means that ancestor was a warm-blooded animal, because cold-blooded animals never have insulation - it would be detrimental to them. So, the very first dinosaur had to have been a warm-blooded, feathered animal. So, knowing that, what’s so special about birds? Really, nothing - they have very few unique features compared with other dinosaurs, and all of them are related to their having evolved the ability to fly. The first birds evolved around 150 million years ago, so the Avialans were a huge clade long before the disaster struck. A velociraptor and a sparrow are astronomically less different than a bat and a dolphin. If bats and dolphins are both still mammals, then sparrows are certainly still dinosaurs. The Chicxulub impactor, a giant asteroid that struck near the tip of the Yucatan Peninsula, caused the extinction of around 80% of all species a bit over 66 million years ago (our dating has improved, too). Many clades became entirely extinct, including pterosaurs and mosasaurs. But there were also many survivors - sometimes hanging in there by just a few species. Mammals had some survivors, and so did dinosaurs. All of the dinosaurian survivors were part of the clade Avialae. The largest group of birds alive before the asteroid strike were the Enantiornithes. Not a single species survived. Instead, a few species of small, flying, ground-nesting and foraging birds in a handful of clades were the survivors. All modern birds descend from them. Birds are dinosaurs - the dinosaurs never did become extinct.
