Question: If it is true that humans came from previously existing, lower lifeforms, why has this evolution not continued?
Answer: Evolution never actually stops - the term refers to a continuous process. Sometimes evolution occurs faster, and sometimes more slowly, but it’s always happening. The term ‘evolution’ in reference to organisms means ‘changes that occur in a population over time.’ This distinguishes it from changes that occur in individuals. A population is a contiguous breeding group of organisms of the same species. Evolution begins when mutations occur, hybridization occurs, or horizontal gene transfer occurs in a single organism in the group. If that change is detrimental, that may mean that the organism doesn’t survive to breed, or breeds less successfully than organisms without that change. So, either immediately or after a few generations, all individuals with that change will be eliminated. This is called ‘purifying’ or ‘negative’ selection. It’s an important part of the evolutionary process, and helps a species maintain its integrity over time. If the change that occurs in the individual is neutral or beneficial, then the organism has a better chance of survival (though bad luck can still strike). It may have more offspring than the others that don’t have the beneficial mutation. (Or the same amount, if the change is neutral). Sometimes a neutral change will proliferate through the population if the one that carries it has other genes that improve its survival potential. A beneficial change will often proliferate much faster, as the individual’s offspring will, in turn, have more breeding success, and so on. So the organism that don’t have the mutation will mate with the ones that do, and their carrier offspring will survive better than the non-carriers, until finally the entire population has the beneficial change. But there isn’t just one of these changes happening at a time - there are typically many of them, being positively and negatively reinforced in the population all at once. This is responsible for the diversity in individuals that you see. Not all deer in an area look the same - some are bigger, some smaller, some more gracile, some sturdier, their coats may be different colors, etc etc. That is the result of the evolutionary process at work. For a species to evolve into an entire new species takes a very long time in most cases. Except when it doesn’t - every once in a while, hybridization (an important part of evolution’s tool chest) can produce a new species practically overnight! And we’ve been privileged to be paying attention in just the right place, at the right time, to see it happen before our very eyes. This new species is fragile, but is expanding its population and appears sturdy. An example of hybrid speciation - evolution in action, right in front of us! Another potential new species is in the process of evolving in the Eastern United States. Presently considered to be ‘coyotes,’ the Eastern Coyote is a species with variable amounts of wolf and dog genes from hybrid matings. (Typically the animals are no less than 60% coyote - usually closer to 80%). From wolves, they gain greater size and better cooperative/pack hunting behaviors. From domestic dogs they gain the ability to understand human behavior and a tolerance for human-modified areas. This makes them ideal predators to take the place of extirpated gray wolves. They can live in our parks and golf courses, and eat the bountiful numbers of rodents, squirrels, and rabbits that proliferate there due to low numbers of other predators. They’re also large enough to take white tail deer fawns. As evolution continues to select them, they will no doubt become better deer hunters, and also be less prone to behavior that puts them in conflict with humans (as those individuals that behave that way are often eliminated from the gene pool). The Western coyote, ancestor of these animals, is smaller, and a solitary hunter that lives only with its mate. Pups stay with their parents only until fully grown, the disperse. The Eastern Coyote is often seen in packs. As for human evolution, there are many examples of our continued changing within populations. Homo sapiens, our species, is only around 300,000 years old. It evolved from Homo antecessor or Homo heidelbergensis (incredibly similar human species, we have no DNA from fossils of course, so identifying the exact ancestor from such similar species is very difficult). This is a forensic reconstruction of Homo antecessor from a skull. As you can see, if this guy were dressed up and walking down the street, you probably wouldn’t blink twice. He’s just not that different from us. But he is not our species. Our species suffered a severe population bottleneck which greatly reduced our genetic diversity. This slowed our evolution, as you definitely get more variety faster with greater genetic diversity. But we mated with several other human species on our way out of Africa, so most of us carry small amounts of genes from Neanderthals, Denisovans, and a third human species we have only genetic evidence of, and no fossils for yet. And the selective process of evolution is responsible for the fact that most Europeans can digest milk sugar (lactose) as adults: but most people in other parts of the world cannot. That’s just one example among many of changes occurring in populations as the result of natural selection. So, the answer to your question is: Your premise is incorrect. The thing you are attempting to use to disprove a proven theory is simply not true. Of course it’s not - you did not notice something no scientist in the world ever noticed. Evolutionary theory is proven for a reason. That reason is the giant mountain of evidence that supports it, and the fact that there is zero evidence that disproves it in any way.

Question: How many bird species were there before and after the extinction of all non-avian dinosaurs (excluding living ones)?
Answer: We haven’t the faintest idea. The smaller and thinner bones are, the less likely they are to fossilize. And some environments can produce fossils, while others simply don’t. Even in environments conducive to fossilization, only a tiny fraction of individuals will actually be fossilized. Tremendous numbers of species have existed that we will never know about. There is simply no way we can. We do know that most clades of birds became extinct when the Chicxulub asteroid struck, just as the non-avian dinosaurs did. One group, the Enantiornithes, was the most abundant and diverse group of birds alive at that time (as far as we know). All gone.

Question: What are some species of animals that are at risk of extinction? Why are they at risk? Which one do you think should be saved first, and why?
Answer: We’re not doing your homework for you. This is obviously a homework question: it’s clear from the wording. So, I’m going to be general. And a bit hyperlexic. ;) Animals at highest risk of extinction are those that are specialized to specific small habitats. Also at risk are those that have, unfortunately, attracted attention from humans as valuable on the market, or which are competing with humans for resources. Additionally, species that live in habitats that are rapidly shrinking are also at risk. In general, the more adaptable a species is, and the wider the variety of habitats it can survive in, the more resilient it is (the less likely it is to become extinct). As to what we should save first - conservation organizations have this one figured out. The animal species that should be prioritized are megafauna and apex predators. They have the greatest impacts on the ecosystems they live in, and their loss would have destructive cascading effects. Additionally, they require vast areas to assure their survival. When you protect large swaths of land to save one huge animal, you also wind up saving everything else that lives there. It’s not that the tiny animal that lives on just a few square acres isn’t as valuable - it’s that conservation of the larger one that needs hundreds of thousands of acres has a lot more impact. It’s also easier to get humans to donate money to save huge, charismatic animals. Humans instinctively think bigger things are more valuable (which is worth more in your mind - a mouse or a whale)? Biodiversity is strength. Ecosystems with fewer species are more susceptible to catastrophic failure from the loss of a single species.

Question: Why are there so many corn snakes and ball pythons for sale at reptile expos?
Answer: They are the most suitable ‘starter’ reptiles for new keepers, and arguably make the best pets out of any reptiles. Corn snakes are the only snakes that are semi- to fully- domesticated. (Ball pythons have too much wild blood coming in as hatchlings are still mass-imported). Both are extremely easy to care for and breed, and come in an nearly endless variety of colors and patterns that combine in interesting and appealing ways. They’re fun to breed, and make ideal family pets. New rare morphs and combinations can have high price tags, which is also appealing to breeders who would love to break even or do even better on their hobby. The presence of huge numbers of these animals, and very few of more challenging and uncommon species reflects the way things should be in the reptile hobby and market. Most people should have one of these animals, and very few (the most experienced) should have more difficult or rare ones.

Name: Donna Fernstrom
Question: Are pet snakes considered as "domesticated snakes" or are they just as wild as any snake?
Answer: I would say that there are good arguments to consider the common corn snake (Pantherophis guttatus) to have a domesticated population in captivity. They have been captive-bred to have specific traits conducive to life in captivity for a very long time now. It’s extremely rare for wild-caught snakes to be kept or bred now, so the captive population is genetically quite isolated. I would say that these arguments don’t really exist for the vast majority of other species of snakes kept in captivity, and that they should still be considered to be captive wildlife. Even ball pythons; because there is a great deal of gene flow from wild snakes into the population still. So: corn snakes, probably domesticated, and at minimum semi-domesticated. Other species: captive wildlife. Other domesticated/semi-domesticated reptiles include leopard geckos, bearded dragons, and crested geckos. (But no other snakes).

Question: I did a resin project and now, the whole room stinks. Will this hurt my pet birds?
Answer: Yes, some resins are absolutely horrifically dangerous for pet birds, and you should find them other lodgings, or set up a fan to blow through the house and out that window (and keep them in the farthest room from it) until every trace of the stink is gone. Read the label on your resin brand CAREFULLY - some resins have an odor, but don’t produce harmful fumes. You need to be extra clear about which one you’re using, and that the chemicals in it are actually safe for birds. Remember that a bird’s respiratory tract is many times more sensitive than a human’s. If your resin says to use in a well-ventilated area, then it may kill your birds. Just being in the same house when someone has overheated non-stick cookware will kill a bird.

Name: Donna Fernstrom
Question: Why haven't we tried to domesticate other species of apes, like bonobos or common chimpanzees?
Answer: Putting aside the rather chilling potential for created a literal slave species, the practical aspects of this are the primary barrier. Chimps are horrifically aggressive and vengeful, and tend to go for the face and genitals with their fangs when angered. They have little impulse-control. Bonobos have sex as a greeting gesture, and whenever upset in any way. Both species are delicate and difficult to keep healthy in captivity. They need specialized diets, or they die as young adults of heart disease. Both species are stronger than humans and dangerous as adults. (Yes, even bonobos). Both species have a very long generational turnover - they have long childhoods, and only have one child at a time, and that only once every five years! (Less often than humans)! We could domesticate sliver foxes in about 60 years because they have litters of 3 to 6 every year, and the pups take only 10 months to reach sexual maturity). Imagine how long it would take to produce a simple temperament change (all that was done with the foxes) in great apes, given how much longer their generational turnover is! Plus, it required tens of thousands of foxes for the experiment (it was a working fur farm). Where and how would you house thousands of chimps or bonobos, and what would you do with the culls? If you were to spend tens of thousands of years domesticating a population of these animals, you would be left with animals that are as intelligent as a five year old child, and docile and trustworthy enough to live in our homes, right? They would have to be declared persons at that point, because we would have eliminated through selective-breeding some of the differences that prevented us from declaring them such. Giving them more patience, a more cooperative nature, increasing their empathy and gentleness… we would turn them into a people. Not human people, but still people. It’s easy for us to declare that chimpanzees, with their penchant for sudden violence, aren’t people. They can’t be trusted outside of an enclosure. They’re more dangerous than lions. But take that aspect away, and what’s left is far too much like us.

Question: How are the new mRNA vaccines more effective than old fashioned vaccines that introduce a tiny part of the virus so that people can build an immunity?
Answer: It’s not clear that they’re NECESSARILY more effective, though they certainly seem to be with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. But they’re definitely at least equally effective. The nifty part about them is that they don’t involve introducing any part of the real virus into your body, which makes them in many respects safer. I was not able to find out which vaccines produced fewer side-effects, because that information seems to be deeply obfuscated. Serious side effects are very rare with any of the vaccines in any case. Perhaps the immunity produced by mRNA vaccines is stronger for COVID-19 because the protein is being produced by your body for several days, so there is more of it there, creating a stronger immune response. The real potential of mRNA vaccines is the ability to use the technology to develop vaccines for things that we normally couldn’t vaccinate for, because they aren’t viruses or bacteria. For example, some types of cancers! mRNA vaccines are being developed to combat some cancers, and are effective after the person has the cancer in question. Cancers hide from your immune system (otherwise they wouldn’t exist). mRNA cancer vaccines can reveal them to your immune system.
